claim: ADP-ribosylation (ADPRylation) is a reversible post-translation modification resulting in the covalent attachment of ADP-ribose (ADPR) moieties on substrate proteins.
source: ADP-ribosylation (ADPRylation) is a reversible post-translation modification resulting in the covalent attachment of ADP-ribose (ADPR) moieties on substrate proteins.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about ADPRylation supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: Naturally occurring protein motifs and domains, including WWEs, PBZs, and macrodomains, act as 'readers' for protein-linked ADPR.
source: Naturally occurring protein motifs and domains, including WWEs, PBZs, and macrodomains, act as 'readers' for protein-linked ADPR.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge about ADPR-binding domains.

claim: PAR Trackers (PAR-Ts) are optimized dimerization-dependent or split-protein reassembly PAR sensors in which a naturally occurring PAR binding domain, WWE, was fused to both halves of dimerization-dependent GFP (ddGFP) or split Nano Luciferase (NanoLuc).
source: Herein, we describe and characterize a set of poly(ADP-ribose) (PAR) Trackers (PAR-Ts)—optimized dimerization-dependent or split-protein reassembly PAR sensors in which a naturally occurring PAR binding domain, WWE, was fused to both halves of dimerization-dependent GFP (ddGFP) or split Nano Luciferase (NanoLuc), respectively.
evidence: This describes the design and construction of the PAR-T sensors developed in this study.

claim: PAR Trackers allow the detection and quantification of PAR levels in extracts, living cells, and living tissues with greater sensitivity, as well as temporal and spatial precision.
source: We demonstrate that these new tools allow the detection and quantification of PAR levels in extracts, living cells, and living tissues with greater sensitivity, as well as temporal and spatial precision.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript demonstrating the sensors' performance in various contexts.

claim: PAR Trackers detect changes in cellular ADPR levels in response to physiological cues (e.g., hormone-dependent induction of adipogenesis without DNA damage).
source: Importantly, these sensors detect changes in cellular ADPR levels in response to physiological cues (e.g., hormone-dependent induction of adipogenesis without DNA damage), as well as xenograft tumor tissues in living mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing PAR-T detection during adipogenesis (Figure 7).

claim: PAR Trackers detect changes in cellular ADPR levels in xenograft tumor tissues in living mice.
source: Importantly, these sensors detect changes in cellular ADPR levels in response to physiological cues (e.g., hormone-dependent induction of adipogenesis without DNA damage), as well as xenograft tumor tissues in living mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing PAR-T detection in xenograft tumors (Figure 8).

claim: Members of the PARP family of ADP-ribosyltransferases (ARTs) function as 'writers' to catalyze the transfer of ADPR moieties from oxidized β-nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) to a variety of amino acids (Asp, Glu, Ser, Arg, and Lys) in substrate proteins.
source: Members of the PARP family of ADP-ribosyltransferases (ARTs) (Amé et al., 2004; Vyas et al., 2013) function as 'writers' to catalyze the transfer of ADPR moieties from oxidized β-nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) to a variety of amino acids (Asp, Glu, Ser, Arg, and Lys) in substrate proteins (Gupte et al., 2017; Lüscher et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mono(ADP-ribosyl) transferases (MARTs) add a single ADPR moiety to their substrates through a process called mono(ADP-ribosyl)ation (MARylation).
source: Mono(ADP-ribosyl) transferases (MARTs) add a single ADPR moiety to their substrates through a process called mono(ADP-ribosyl)ation (MARylation) (Challa et al., 2021), whereas poly(ADP-ribosyl) transferases (PARPs) add branched or linear chains of multiple ADPR moieties through a process called poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation (PARylation) (Gupte et al., 2017; Lüscher et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Poly(ADP-ribosyl) transferases (PARPs) add branched or linear chains of multiple ADPR moieties through a process called poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation (PARylation).
source: Mono(ADP-ribosyl) transferases (MARTs) add a single ADPR moiety to their substrates through a process called mono(ADP-ribosyl)ation (MARylation) (Challa et al., 2021), whereas poly(ADP-ribosyl) transferases (PARPs) add branched or linear chains of multiple ADPR moieties through a process called poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation (PARylation) (Gupte et al., 2017; Lüscher et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Site-specific ADPRylation of substrate proteins by PARP enzymes can alter the biochemical or biophysical properties of the substrate protein.
source: Site-specific ADPRylation of substrate proteins by PARP enzymes can have important functional consequences, including alteration of the biochemical or biophysical properties of the substrate protein or creation of new binding sites for ADPR binding domains (ARBDs) that drive protein-protein interactions (Gibson and Kraus, 2012; Gupte et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Site-specific ADPRylation of substrate proteins by PARP enzymes can create new binding sites for ADPR binding domains (ARBDs) that drive protein-protein interactions.
source: Site-specific ADPRylation of substrate proteins by PARP enzymes can have important functional consequences, including alteration of the biochemical or biophysical properties of the substrate protein or creation of new binding sites for ADPR binding domains (ARBDs) that drive protein-protein interactions (Gibson and Kraus, 2012; Gupte et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ADPRylation can control DNA repair, DNA replication, gene expression, and RNA biology, as well as inflammatory responses and cell differentiation.
source: As such, ADPRylation can control a wide variety of cellular and biological processes, including DNA repair, DNA replication, gene expression, and RNA biology, as well as inflammatory responses and cell differentiation (Challa et al., 2021; Gibson and Kraus, 2012; Gupte et al., 2017; Lüscher et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ADPR binding domains (ARBDs) function as 'readers' of the various forms of protein-linked ADPR (MAR, PAR, branched, terminal residue, etc.).
source: These ARBDs function as 'readers' of the various forms of protein-linked ADPR (MAR, PAR, branched, terminal residue, etc.).
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge about ADPR-binding domains.

claim: ARBDs include PAR-binding motifs (PBMs), macrodomains, PAR-binding zinc fingers (PBZs), and WWE domains.
source: They include PAR-binding motifs (PBMs), macrodomains, PAR-binding zinc fingers (PBZs), and WWE domains (Ahel et al., 2008; Feijs et al., 2013; Gagné et al., 2008; Karras et al., 2005; Pleschke et al., 2000; Rack et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Macrodomains recognize free ADPR, as well as the terminal ADPR moieties in PAR, allowing them to bind to both MAR and PAR.
source: Macrodomains recognize free ADPR, as well as the terminal ADPR moieties in PAR, allowing them to bind to both MAR and PAR (Karras et al., 2005; Timinszky et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PBZ domains recognize branched forms of PAR.
source: PBZ domains recognize branched forms of PAR (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: WWE domains recognize the iso-ADPR linkages joining ADPR monomers, restricting their binding to PAR.
source: WWE domains recognize the iso-ADPR linkages joining ADPR monomers, restricting their binding to PAR (Kang et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 'Eraser' enzymes, including PAR glycohydrolase (PARG) and ADP-ribosylhydrolase 3 (ARH3), recognize specific ADPR modifications through the ARBDs and catalyze PAR chain degradation through endo- and exoglycocidic activities.
source: In addition to the 'writers' and 'readers,' 'eraser' enzymes, including PAR glycohydrolase (PARG) and ADP-ribosylhydrolase 3 (ARH3), recognize specific ADPR modifications through the ARBDs and catalyze PAR chain degradation through endo- and exoglycocidic activities.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PARG and ARH3 activities leave the terminal ADPR moiety attached to the acceptor amino acid residue of the substrate.
source: Their activities leave the terminal ADPR moiety attached to the acceptor amino acid residue of the substrate (Barkauskaite et al., 2013; Niere et al., 2012; Oka et al., 2006; Slade et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The anti-PAR monoclonal antibody 10H binds to PAR chains longer than ten ADPR units.
source: Instead, the PARP field has relied on the anti-PAR monoclonal antibody 10H, which binds to PAR chains longer than ten ADPR units (Kawamitsu et al., 1984).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The anti-PAR monoclonal antibody 10H has left the field blind to mono- and oligo(ADP-ribosyl)ation.
source: Although useful, this antibody has left the field blind to mono- and oligo(ADP-ribosyl)ation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the specificity of the 10H antibody for long PAR chains.

claim: ADPRylation is a rapid process that can occur within minutes and can be removed by various 'erasers' including ARH3 and PARG.
source: In fact, ADPRylation is a rapid process that can occur within minutes and can be removed by various 'erasers' including ARH3 and PARG (Barkauskaite et al., 2013; Gupte et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The WWE domain from RNF146 and macrodomain from AF1521 performed well in specifically recognizing PARylated PARP-1.
source: We observed that of all the ARBD-ddGFP pairs tested, the WWE domain from RNF146, macrodomain from AF1521, and a combination of these two performed well in specifically recognizing PARylated PARP-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: PAR-T sensors recognized PARylated-PARP-1, but not MARylated PARP-3, or the precursors of ADPR.
source: These sensors recognized PARylated-PARP-1, but not MARylated PARP-3, or the precursors of ADPR (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: PAR-T ddGFP sensors can specifically recognize PAR and exhibit a good dynamic range in vitro.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the PAR-T ddGFP sensors can specifically recognize PAR, and that they exhibit a good dynamic range in vitro.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: WWE-based ddGFP PAR-T sensor detected PARP-1 activation in live-cell imaging.
source: When compared to ddGFP alone, ddGFP-conjugated to WWE detected PARP-1 activation in live-cell imaging (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The WWE-macrodomain combination sensor failed to recognize PAR in cells.
source: Interestingly, even though the WWE-macrodomain combination sensor was able to detect PAR in vitro, this sensor combination failed to recognize PAR in cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Using the WWE-based ddGFP PAR-T sensor, PAR accumulation after H2O2-treatment was detected in real time.
source: Using the WWE-based ddGFP PAR-T sensor, we were able to detect accumulation of PAR after H2O2-treatment in real time.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Treatment with PARP inhibitor blocked PAR accumulation after H2O2-treatment.
source: Treatment with PARP inhibitor blocked this accumulation (Figure 2C and D; Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: PAR levels vary spatially in groups of cells in 3D cancer spheroids.
source: We observed a heterogeneous distribution of PAR throughout the spheroid, which was inhibited by the PARP inhibitor, Niraparib (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: PAR levels in cells at the core of the spheroids are relatively resistant to Niraparib treatment compared to cells in the outer layer of the spheroid.
source: The results indicate that the PAR levels in cells at the core of the spheroids are relatively resistant to Niraparib treatment, since the PAR levels in these cells decrease at a lower rate compared to the PAR levels in the cells in the outer layer of the spheroid (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The PAR-T-ddGFP sensor can be used for live-cell imaging to evaluate spatial and temporal changes in PARylation in cancer cells.
source: These results show that the PAR-T-ddGFP sensor can be used for live-cell imaging to evaluate spatial and temporal changes in PARylation in cancer cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: WWE domains consistently performed better in detecting an increase in PAR levels with PARG inhibitor treatment and a decrease in PAR levels with a PARP inhibitor treatment using either cell lysates or live cells.
source: As before, the WWE domains consistently performed better in detecting an increase in PAR levels with PARG inhibitor treatment and a decrease in PAR levels with a PARP inhibitor treatment using either cell lysates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) or live cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The signal intensity from the split firefly luciferase-based PAR-T sensors were ~10,000-fold less than intact firefly luciferase.
source: Although split firefly luciferase-based approaches were capable of detecting signals from cells in vitro, the signal intensity from the split firefly luciferase-based PAR-T sensors were ~10,000-fold less than intact firefly luciferase, which makes it difficult to use this sensor in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing split and intact firefly luciferase.

claim: The luminescence of PAR-T NanoLuc is only 30-fold lower than intact firefly luciferase.
source: Moreover, the luminescence of PAR-T NanoLuc is only 30-fold lower than intact firefly luciferase (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: PARP-1 depletion reduced the luminescence from PAR-T NanoLuc with little effect on the luminescence of firefly luciferase.
source: PARP-1 depletion reduced the luminescence from PAR-T NanoLuc with little effect on the luminescence of firefly luciferase (Figure 4E-G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: Knockdown of PARP-2 had no effect on luminescence from PAR-T NanoLuc.
source: Interestingly, knockdown of PARP-2 had no effect on luminescence from PAR-T NanoLuc.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: The luminescent PAR-T NanoLuc sensor is highly sensitive and can be used to detect PAR in 1000 cells with a dynamic range of approximately threefold (minimum to maximum).
source: Nevertheless, the luminescent PAR-T NanoLuc sensor is highly sensitive and can be used to detect PAR in 1000 cells with a dynamic range of approximately threefold (minimum to maximum) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: UV radiation-induced PARP-1 activation as assessed by an accumulation of PAR on Western blots.
source: We observed that UV radiation-induced PARP-1 activation as assessed by an accumulation of PAR on Western blots (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: UV radiation-induced PARP-1 activation was further enhanced by inhibition of PARG.
source: This was further enhanced by inhibition of PARG, whereas inhibition of PARP-1 blocked the UV-induced PARP-1 activation (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Inhibition of PARP-1 blocked the UV-induced PARP-1 activation.
source: This was further enhanced by inhibition of PARG, whereas inhibition of PARP-1 blocked the UV-induced PARP-1 activation (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: UV radiation of PARG inhibitor-treated cells enhanced PAR-T luminescence.
source: UV radiation of PARG inhibitor-treated cells enhanced PAR-T luminescence, whereas UV radiation of PARP inhibitor-treated cells reduced the PAR-T luminescence (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: UV radiation of PARP inhibitor-treated cells reduced the PAR-T luminescence.
source: UV radiation of PARG inhibitor-treated cells enhanced PAR-T luminescence, whereas UV radiation of PARP inhibitor-treated cells reduced the PAR-T luminescence (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: UV-mediated increases in PARP-1 activation were more spontaneous in PARG inhibitor-treated cells.
source: Interestingly, UV-mediated increases in PARP-1 activation were more spontaneous in PARG inhibitor-treated cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Western blotting with WWE-Fc had the highest dynamic range for detection of PAR (eightfold).
source: We found that Western blotting with WWE-Fc had the highest dynamic range for detection of PAR (eightfold), but the dynamic range of live-cell luciferase assay with PAR-T NanoLuc was comparable (sixfold) (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The dynamic range of live-cell luciferase assay with PAR-T NanoLuc was comparable to Western blotting with WWE-Fc (sixfold).
source: We found that Western blotting with WWE-Fc had the highest dynamic range for detection of PAR (eightfold), but the dynamic range of live-cell luciferase assay with PAR-T NanoLuc was comparable (sixfold) (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: PAR-T ddGFP in a modified fluorescence assay had a larger dynamic range than PAR antibody in an ELISA (6-fold vs. 3.5-fold) when the assays were performed using immobilized PAR.
source: While PAR-T ddGFP in a modified fluorescence assay had a larger dynamic range than PAR antibody in an ELISA (6-fold vs. 3.5-fold) when the assays were performed using immobilized PAR, it had a lower dynamic range when used for live-cell imaging (4.4-fold).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and 6F.

claim: PAR-T ddGFP had a lower dynamic range when used for live-cell imaging (4.4-fold) compared to immobilized PAR assays.
source: While PAR-T ddGFP in a modified fluorescence assay had a larger dynamic range than PAR antibody in an ELISA (6-fold vs. 3.5-fold) when the assays were performed using immobilized PAR, it had a lower dynamic range when used for live-cell imaging (4.4-fold).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The performance of PAR-T ddGFP in live cells is comparable to that of an immunofluorescence assay with WWE-Fc (4.4-fold vs. 5-fold).
source: Nevertheless, the performance of PAR-T ddGFP in live cells is comparable to that of an immunofluorescence assay with WWE-Fc (4.4-fold vs. 5-fold).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: PARP-1 catalytic activity decreases during the initial differentiation of preadipocytes.
source: We previously showed that PARP-1 catalytic activity decreases during the initial differentiation of preadipocytes (Huang et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2017; Ryu et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature from the authors' group.

claim: A decrease in the signal from PAR-T NanoLuc was observed by 12 hr of differentiation and a greater reduction in PAR-T NanoLuc signal by 24 hr of differentiation.
source: We observed a decrease in the signal from PAR-T NanoLuc by 12 hr of differentiation and a greater reduction in PAR-T NanoLuc signal by 24 hr of differentiation (Figure 7), consistent with our previous observation that PARP-1 activation decreases precipitously during adipogenesis (Huang et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2017; Ryu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: PAR-T NanoLuc sensor can be used to study physiological changes in PAR levels during biological processes, such as adipogenesis.
source: These results further highlight the high sensitivity of PAR-T NanoLuc sensor, which can be used to study physiological changes in PAR levels during biological processes, such as adipogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 7.

claim: An increase in PAR levels was detected with the PAR-T NanoLuc sensor when the gamma-irradiated mice were treated with PARG inhibitor.
source: Similar to the in vitro experiments, we detected an increase in PAR levels with the PAR-T NanoLuc sensor when the gamma-irradiated mice were treated with PARG inhibitor, but the signal was decreased when the gamma-irradiated mice were treated with PARP inhibitor (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The PAR-T NanoLuc signal was decreased when the gamma-irradiated mice were treated with PARP inhibitor.
source: Similar to the in vitro experiments, we detected an increase in PAR levels with the PAR-T NanoLuc sensor when the gamma-irradiated mice were treated with PARG inhibitor, but the signal was decreased when the gamma-irradiated mice were treated with PARP inhibitor (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PAR accumulation was readily detected in the breast cancer cells injected into the mice in the absence of treatment.
source: PAR accumulation was readily detected in the breast cancer cells injected into the mice in the absence of treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: Upon treatment with PARG inhibitor, the luminescence from PAR-T NanoLuc increased significantly by 6 hr and then diminished by 24 hr.
source: Upon treatment with PARG inhibitor, the luminescence from PAR-T NanoLuc increased significantly by 6 hr and then diminished by 24 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: The PAR-T NanoLuc sensor has sufficient sensitivity to detect dynamic changes in PAR production in tissues of living animals in vivo.
source: These results demonstrate that the PAR-T NanoLuc sensor has sufficient sensitivity to detect dynamic changes in PAR production in tissues of living animals in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dimerization-dependent GFP is a genetically encoded sensor that was initially developed to study protein interactions.
source: Dimerization-dependent GFP is a genetically encoded sensor that was initially developed to study protein interactions (Alford et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the ddGFP system, a pair containing a quenched GFP (ddGFPA) and a nonfluorogenic GFP (ddGFPB) form a heterodimer with improved fluorescence.
source: In this system, a pair containing a quenched GFP (ddGFPA) and a nonfluorogenic GFP (ddGFPB) form a heterodimer with improved fluorescence (Alford et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The reversible complementation of ddGFP pairs, unlike irreversible split fluorophores, is ideal to monitor dynamic signaling events, such as PARylation.
source: The reversible complementation of ddGFP pairs, unlike irreversible split fluorophores, is ideal to monitor dynamic signaling events, such as PARylation (Villalobos et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature and logical inference.

claim: Furman et al., 2011 made a bivalent split-protein PAR-specific sensor encompassing the PBZ modules of APLF attached to each half of split firefly luciferase.
source: In previous work, Furman et al., 2011 made a bivalent split-protein PAR-specific sensor encompassing the PBZ modules of APLF (residues 376–441) (Ahel et al., 2008) attached to each half of split firefly luciferase (split-Fluc) (Furman et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The APLF PBZ-split firefly luciferase sensor allows the detection of PAR from biochemical reactions and cell lysates.
source: This tool allows the detection of PAR from biochemical reactions and cell lysates (Furman et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Krastev et al., 2018 made an APLF PBZ domain-fused split fluorescence sensor based on Venus fluorescent protein to detect PAR.
source: Krastev et al., 2018 also made an APLF PBZ domain-fused split fluorescence sensor based on Venus fluorescent protein to detect PAR (Krastev et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Serebrovskaya et al., 2020 developed FRET-based PAR sensors by fusing the WWE domain from RNF146 to the Torquoise2 and Venus fluorescent proteins.
source: In a recent study, Serebrovskaya et al., 2020 developed FRET-based PAR sensors by fusing the WWE domain from RNF146 to the Torquoise2 and Venus fluorescent proteins (Serebrovskaya et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Previously developed PAR sensors are irreversible, thus limiting their use for measuring dynamic changes in PAR levels.
source: However, the aforementioned approaches for PAR sensors have the following limitations. (1) they are irreversible, thus limiting their use for measuring dynamic changes in PAR levels, (2) the requirement for measuring filtered light emissions in FRET-based sensors results in low signal intensities and narrow dynamic ranges that limit their utility in a variety of applications, (3) PBZ domains detect branched PAR chains synthesized predominantly by PARP-2 (Chen et al., 2018), and (4) they are unable to measure PAR levels in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of previously developed sensors.

claim: The requirement for measuring filtered light emissions in FRET-based sensors results in low signal intensities and narrow dynamic ranges that limit their utility in a variety of applications.
source: However, the aforementioned approaches for PAR sensors have the following limitations. (1) they are irreversible, thus limiting their use for measuring dynamic changes in PAR levels, (2) the requirement for measuring filtered light emissions in FRET-based sensors results in low signal intensities and narrow dynamic ranges that limit their utility in a variety of applications, (3) PBZ domains detect branched PAR chains synthesized predominantly by PARP-2 (Chen et al., 2018), and (4) they are unable to measure PAR levels in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of FRET-based sensors.

claim: PBZ domains detect branched PAR chains synthesized predominantly by PARP-2.
source: However, the aforementioned approaches for PAR sensors have the following limitations. (1) they are irreversible, thus limiting their use for measuring dynamic changes in PAR levels, (2) the requirement for measuring filtered light emissions in FRET-based sensors results in low signal intensities and narrow dynamic ranges that limit their utility in a variety of applications, (3) PBZ domains detect branched PAR chains synthesized predominantly by PARP-2 (Chen et al., 2018), and (4) they are unable to measure PAR levels in vivo.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Previously developed PAR sensors are unable to measure PAR levels in vivo.
source: However, the aforementioned approaches for PAR sensors have the following limitations. (1) they are irreversible, thus limiting their use for measuring dynamic changes in PAR levels, (2) the requirement for measuring filtered light emissions in FRET-based sensors results in low signal intensities and narrow dynamic ranges that limit their utility in a variety of applications, (3) PBZ domains detect branched PAR chains synthesized predominantly by PARP-2 (Chen et al., 2018), and (4) they are unable to measure PAR levels in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of reported in vivo applications of previously developed sensors.

claim: Assembly of dimerization-dependent fluorophores and split luciferase proteins are reversible and have a higher signal intensity.
source: To overcome these limitations, we developed a set of PAR sensors in which ARBDs are fused to ddGFP or split luciferase. Assembly of dimerization-dependent fluorophores and split luciferase proteins are reversible and have a higher signal intensity (Alford et al., 2012; Luker et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Fluorescent sensors are not optimal for use in vivo due to high auto-fluorescence of tissue.
source: For example, fluorescent sensors are not optimal for use in vivo due to high auto-fluorescence of tissue; thus, we had to use a luminescent sensor to increase the sensitivity of PAR detection in vivo.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the limitations of fluorescent sensors in vivo.

claim: The luminescence of split luciferase is typically 100- to 1000-fold less than intact luciferase.
source: Although intact luciferase can be used in cells as reporter, achieving usable signals from split luciferase is technically challenging because (1) it is difficult to express, (2) the luminescence of split luciferase is typically 100- to 1000-fold less than intact luciferase, and (3) the wavelength emitted by luciferase exhibits poor penetration in tissues.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the properties of split luciferase.

claim: The wavelength emitted by luciferase exhibits poor penetration in tissues.
source: Although intact luciferase can be used in cells as reporter, achieving usable signals from split luciferase is technically challenging because (1) it is difficult to express, (2) the luminescence of split luciferase is typically 100- to 1000-fold less than intact luciferase, and (3) the wavelength emitted by luciferase exhibits poor penetration in tissues.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the properties of luciferase.

claim: NanoLuc is the smallest and brightest luciferase available.
source: To this end, we optimized several aspects of the sensor to achieve the highest sensitivity: (1) we used NanoLuc, the smallest and brightest luciferase available (Wang et al., 2020), (2) we added LSSmOrange to stabilize the C-terminal fragment of NanoLuc (Schaub et al., 2015), (3) we used the Nano-Glo live cell substrate to be able to perform these assays in live cells, (4) we used Dox-inducible constructs to avoid any effects of expression of these constructs on cell viability, and (5) we developed a dual luciferase assay to quantify PAR levels more accurately.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: LSSmOrange was added to stabilize the C-terminal fragment of NanoLuc.
source: To this end, we optimized several aspects of the sensor to achieve the highest sensitivity: (1) we used NanoLuc, the smallest and brightest luciferase available (Wang et al., 2020), (2) we added LSSmOrange to stabilize the C-terminal fragment of NanoLuc (Schaub et al., 2015), (3) we used the Nano-Glo live cell substrate to be able to perform these assays in live cells, (4) we used Dox-inducible constructs to avoid any effects of expression of these constructs on cell viability, and (5) we developed a dual luciferase assay to quantify PAR levels more accurately.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The blue-shifted emission of NanoLuc (at 460 nm) diffuses rapidly in tissues, and hence, it is not optimal for imaging deep tissues.
source: The blue-shifted emission of NanoLuc (at 460 nm) diffuses rapidly in tissues, and hence, it is not optimal for imaging deep tissues (Schaub et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: LSSmOrange fluorescent protein has a higher fluorescence quantum yield that is compatible for excitation by the light emitted by NanoLuc.
source: Therefore, we fused the C-terminal domain of NanoLuc with LSSmOrange fluorescent protein (red-shifted GFP variant), which has a higher fluorescence quantum yield that is compatible for excitation by the light emitted by NanoLuc.
evidence: This is based on the properties of LSSmOrange and its compatibility with NanoLuc.

claim: Upon addition of the luciferase substrate, the bioluminescence energy from NanoLuc excites the LSSmOrange fluorophore, shifting the emission energy to 570 nm via BRET reaction.
source: Upon addition of the luciferase substrate, the bioluminescence energy from NanoLuc excites the LSSmOrange fluorophore, shifting the emission energy to 570 nm via BRET reaction (Schaub et al., 2015).
